newsitem.title: USA: US export credit, EEP plans in line for FY97 cuts.
newsitem.headline: US export credit, EEP plans in line for FY97 cuts.

text.p: The major U.S. agricultural export subsidy and export credit programs were in line for significant funding cuts under bills waiting for floor votes in the House of Representatives and Senate.
Both bills were due for debate next week in Congress.

The appropriations committee in each chamber has voted, as part of drafting a disaster-relief bill, to restrict the export credit program to $3.5 billion this fiscal year, a $2 billion reduction. The House panel would limit ag export subsidies to $10 million, the Senate panel to $50 million.
Congress originally voted to give the Export Enhancement Program $100 million for fiscal 1997, which ends September 30.

Although the bills were subject to amendment during floor debate, cuts appeared likely because lawmakers usually are loath, during floor debate, to second-guess the course plotted by the committees with jurisdiction over issues.
There was disagreement over the Conservation Reserve. The House committee voted to cap new enrollments this year at 14 million acres. The Senate proposed no limit.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman opposed the acreage cap as well as funding cuts for the export programs.
Private consultant Bill Lesher said the long run of strong prices and tight supplies would encourage Congress to curtail the export programs.
"The idea that you're going to need these programs in this kind of year isn't going to happen," Lesher said.
"It (the cuts) probably saves other agriculture programs from being reduced with no harm to export numbers."
Lesher said he was dubious the cap on Conservation Reserve spending would survive. As a large change in farm programs, it was certain to arouse opposition, he said.

Representative George Nethercutt said in an interview that he would try to derail the acreage cap on the House floor. Nethercutt, Washington state Republican, lost, 26-22, in the Appropriations Committee when he tried to delete the cap.

This time, Nethercutt said, he would ask the Rules Committee to guarantee him the opportunity to strike the cap as a violation of House rules against using appropriations bills to make statutory changes.
"I think I'll be the lead on it again," he said. "It (the cap) is not in the Senate bill, which is a factor," in stirring sentiment against it.

The Senate version of the disaster bill included a provision that Democratic leaders said would effectively eliminate the crop insurance program in the event there was no agreement of federal funding for fiscal 1998.

The bill included language to automatically fund federal programs at 98 percent of this year's levels. According to Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota, the formula would put crop insurance out of action because it would make sales commissions so small there would be no incentive for sales.
